summary: Describes GSMPv3, an asymmetric protocol letting external controllers set up and maintain state in label switches such as ATM, frame relay or MPLS switches. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: GSMP puts an outside computer in charge of a label switch. The switch is the one that forwards packets, but it waits to be told: which incoming label goes out of which outgoing label, how much bandwidth to reserve, which labels it may use, and what its counters should report. Every request carries a number so the reply can be matched, and a failure comes back with a code that says what went wrong.

questions: how does gsmp control a switch
what is the gsmp adjacency protocol
subtitle: A master-slave protocol that lets an external controller set up connections, resources and ports on a label switch.

tldr.problem: A label switch such as an ATM, frame relay or MPLS switch normally decides for itself how to set up forwarding state, so an operator who wants a particular connection, a particular quality of service or a particular set of statistics has to go through whatever the vendor's own tools provide.
tldr.mechanism: GSMP makes the switch a slave: a controller sends request messages that create, move and delete branches, manage ports and labels, reserve resources and fetch statistics, and the switch answers with a success or a failure code.
tldr.outcome: The controller holds the state and the switch holds the data plane, and the two keep each other honest through an adjacency protocol, a port session number, and a transaction identifier on every message.

today:
RFC 3292 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines the General Switch Management Protocol version 3.

The document requires that any use of GSMP over an IP network run over TCP/IP with the security considerations of the GSMP encapsulation document, and it records that the protocol is asymmetric, with the controller as master and the switch as slave, and that the partitioning of a switch is static and set up before GSMP is run.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The General Switch Management Protocol is a general purpose protocol to control a label switch. It allows a controller to establish and release connections across the switch, add and delete leaves on a multicast connection, manage switch ports, request configuration information, request and delete reservation of switch resources, and request statistics. It also allows the switch to inform the controller of asynchronous events such as a link going down.

The protocol is asymmetric, the controller being the master and the switch the slave. Multiple switches may be controlled by a single controller, using multiple instantiations of the protocol over separate control connections, and a switch may be controlled by more than one controller by using the technique of partitioning.

A physical switch can be partitioned into several virtual switches, called partitions. In this version of GSMP the partitioning is static and occurs before GSMP is run. The partitions of a physical switch are isolated from each other by the implementation, and the controller assumes that the resources allocated to a partition are at all times available to that partition. A partition appears to its controller as a label switch, and the resources allocated to it appear as if they were the actual physical resources of the partition. For example, if the bandwidth of a port were divided among several partitions, each partition would appear to the controller to have its own independent port.

GSMP controls a partitioned switch through a partition identifier carried in every GSMP message. Each partition has a one-to-one control relationship with its own logical controller entity, and GSMP independently maintains adjacency between each controller and partition pair.

Kinds of label switch include frame or cell switches that support connection oriented switching, using the exact match-forwarding algorithm based on labels attached to incoming cells or frames. A switch is assumed to contain multiple ports, and each port is a combination of one input port and one output port. Some GSMP requests refer to the port as a whole, while others are specific to the input port or the output port. Cells or labelled frames arrive at the switch on incoming labelled channels at an input port, and depart on labelled channels from an output port.

A switch may support multiple label types, but each switch port can support only one label type, and the label type supported by a given port is indicated by the switch to the controller in a port configuration message. Label types include ATM, Frame Relay, MPLS Generic and FEC Labels. A connection across a switch is formed by connecting an incoming labelled channel to one or more outgoing labelled channels, and connections are referenced by the input port on which they originate and the label values of their incoming labelled channel.

GSMP supports point-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections. A multipoint-to-point connection is specified by establishing multiple point-to-point connections, each specifying the same output branch, and a multipoint-to-multipoint connection by establishing multiple point-to-multipoint trees each specifying the same output branches.
sections.plainLanguage: One switch can be split into several independent pieces, each with its own controller, so that one operator cannot disturb another's connections. To the controller, each piece appears as a switch of its own, with its own ports and its own labels.

sections.title: The GSMP Packet Format
sections.content:
All GSMP messages, except the adjacency protocol message, have a common header. It carries the Version, the Message Type, the Result and the Code in the first four octets; the Partition ID and the Transaction Identifier in the next three; and then an I flag, a SubMessage Number and a Length in the following four octets, followed by the message body. The Version should be set by the sender to the protocol version negotiated by the adjacency protocol.

The Message Type field names the message. GSMP messages fall into the classes Connection Management, Reservation Management, Port Management, State and Statistics, Configuration, Quality of Service and Events, plus messages belonging to an Abstract or Resource Model extension. Each class has a number of message types, and one Message Type is allocated to the adjacency protocol.

The Result field in a request message indicates whether a response is required if the outcome is successful: NoSuccessAck means the request does not expect a response, and AckAll means a response is expected. In both cases a failure response must be generated if the request fails. For State and Statistics and Configuration request messages a value of NoSuccessAck is ignored and the request is handled as if it were AckAll. This facility was added to reduce control traffic where the controller periodically checks that the state in the switch is correct.

In a response message the Result field can have three values: Success, More and Failure. The Success and More results both indicate success, and all messages belonging to the same success response share the Transaction Identifier. Success indicates a success response that may be contained in a single message or be the final message of a response spanning several messages. More indicates that the message, either request or response, exceeds the maximum transmission unit of the data link and that further messages will follow. ReturnReceipt is a result used in Events to indicate that an acknowledgement is required, and it is the default for events that the controller will not acknowledge. The result field is not used in an adjacency protocol message.

The Code field gives further information about the result. It is mostly used to pass an error code in a failure response, but can also give further information in a success response or an event message. In a request message the Code field is not used and is set to zero, while in an adjacency protocol message it determines the function of the message.

The Partition ID associates the command with a specific switch partition. Its format is not defined in GSMP, and if desired it can be divided into sub-identifiers, for example a 6-bit partition number and a 2-bit sub-identifier, which would allow a switch to support 64 partitions with 4 available identifiers per partition. The Transaction Identifier associates a request message with its response message: the controller may select any value for a request, and a response copies the value from the message it answers, while for event messages it should be set to zero.

The I flag and the SubMessage Number together handle a message too long for the link. When the message is segmented, each segment carries a submessage number showing its position, and if it is the first submessage in a sequence the I flag is set and the field holds the total count of segments. The Length field is the length of the GSMP message including its header and the defined body, and the length of any additional data appended to the end should be included in it.

Switch ports are described by a 32-bit port number, assigned by the switch, which may structure the 32 bits into opaque sub-fields that mean something to the physical structure of the switch, such as slot and port. A port in the same physical location always has the same port number, even across power cycles, and the internal structure is opaque to GSMP. Each switch port also maintains a port session number assigned by the switch, and a message with an incorrect port session number must be rejected, which is how the controller detects a link failure and keeps states synchronised. Except for the adjacency protocol message, no GSMP messages may be sent across the link until the adjacency protocol has achieved synchronisation, and any GSMP messages received on a link that does not have state synchronisation must be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with the same small header: which version, which kind of message, whether it worked, and a number that ties the reply to the request. A long message is split into numbered pieces, and the pieces are reassembled by the switch.

sections.title: Connection Management Messages
sections.content:
Connection management messages are the ones that create and destroy the forwarding state. For all of them except Delete Branches, the success response is a copy of the request message returned with the Result field indicating success, and the Code field is not used in a success response. The failure response is a copy of the request returned with a Result field indicating failure.

No distinction is made between point-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections. By default, the first Add Branch message for a particular input port and input label establishes a point-to-point connection, and the second Add Branch message with the same input port and input label converts the connection to a point-to-multipoint connection with two branches. To avoid possible inefficiency with some switch designs, a Multicast Flag is provided: if the controller knows that a new connection is point-to-multipoint when it establishes the first branch, it may indicate this in the flag, and subsequent Add Branch messages with the same input port and input label will add further branches. Using the Delete Branch message on a point-to-multipoint connection with two branches leaves a point-to-point connection, and using it on a point-to-point connection deletes that connection. There is no concept of a connection with zero output branches, and all connections are unidirectional, from one input labelled channel to one or more output labelled channels.

The Add Branch message establishes a connection or adds an additional branch to an existing one, and may also be used to check the connection state stored in the switch. The connection is specified by the Input Port and Input Label fields, the output branch by the Output Port and Output Label fields, and the quality of service requirements by the QoS Model Selector and Service Selector fields.

Three flags refine the request. The Multicast flag is a hint that the connection is likely to be point-to-multipoint or multipoint-to-point, with separate bits for the input branch and the output branch, and setting both indicates a likely multipoint-to-multipoint connection. It is used only when establishing the first branch, and on such connections it should be ignored; some switches use a different data structure for multicast connections, and the flag stops the switch from building a point-to-point structure for the first branch of a multicast connection that would have to be deleted and reconfigured when the second branch arrives.

The Bi-directional flag applies only to Add Branch and may only be used when establishing a point-to-point connection. If set, it requests two unidirectional connections, one forward and one reverse, and is equivalent to two Add Branch messages. The reverse direction originates at the input port specified by the Output Port field on the label specified by the Output Label field, and departs from the output port specified by the Input Port field on the label specified by the Input Label field. In all future messages the two unidirectional connections must be handled separately, and there is no bi-directional delete message, though a single Delete Branches message with two Delete Branch elements may be used.

The Connection Replace flag also applies only to Add Branch, and is used where the creation of multipoint-to-point connections is undesirable, for example POTS applications where fan-in is meaningless. If it is set, the new connection replaces any existing connection if the label is already in use at the same output port, which lets a single command work as either a Move Branch message or a combination of Delete Branch and Add Branch. This supports existing 64k call handling applications such as emulating 64k voice switches. Its use is optional and must be pre-configured in the Port Management message, and it must not be set if the Multicast or Bi-directional flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: Add Branch is the workhorse: it says that the packets arriving on this label at this port should leave on that label at that port. Sending it again for the same incoming label adds another exit, which is how a multicast tree is built. The flags let the controller hint at what kind of connection it wants, so the switch can build the right structure the first time.

sections.title: Port and Configuration Management
sections.content:
Port management messages cover the ports themselves. The Port Management message is used for administrative and operational control of a port, with a Function field that indicates such actions as Bring Up, Reset Input Port and others, and the switch reports the result of the action. The Label Range message tells the controller which label values the switch can use, and the Label Range message includes a description of the label type in use on the port, so that the controller knows how to interpret the label values it is given.

Configuration messages set the parameters of the switch and of its ports. The Switch Configuration message carries the general configuration and the configuration of the switch itself, including the QoS configuration in use. The Port Configuration message describes a port, and a PortType Specific Data section carries the data particular to the kind of port, such as a label switch port, an ATM port or a frame relay port. The All Ports Configuration message applies a configuration to every port of a given type, and the Service Configuration message configures a service.

State and statistics messages let the controller read what the switch is doing. The Connection Activity message reports which connections are active, and the statistics messages report port statistics, connection statistics and QoS class statistics. The Report Connection State message reports the state of a set of connections.

Event messages are the asynchronous ones, generated by the switch rather than requested by the controller. They cover a port coming up, a port going down, an invalid label, a new port appearing, a dead port, and an adjacency update. The controller can be required to acknowledge event messages, but by default does not do so, and the switch indicates that an acknowledgement is required by setting the Result field to ReturnReceipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Besides creating connections, the controller can ask the switch what its ports are doing, can tell it which labels it may use, can set the configuration of the switch and of each port, and can read the counters. The switch also volunteers information when something changes, such as a port failing, and those event messages can be sent in a form that asks the controller to acknowledge them.

sections.title: The Service Model and Quality of Service
sections.content:
In general a connection is established with a certain quality of service. This version of GSMP includes a default QoS Configuration and additionally allows the negotiation of alternative, optional QoS configurations. The default QoS Configuration includes three QoS Models: a Service Model, a Simple Abstract Model using strict priorities, and a QoS Profile Model.

The Service Model is based on service definitions found external to GSMP, such as those in Integrated Services or the ATM service categories. Each connection is assigned a specific service that defines the handling of the connection by the switch, and traffic parameters and traffic controls may be assigned to the connection depending on the assigned service. The document defines the services it knows about: the ATM Forum service categories, Integrated Services, MPLS CR-LDP, Frame Relay and DiffServ, and for each of them the traffic parameters that can be expressed.

In the Simple Abstract Model, a connection is assigned a priority when it is established. It may be assumed that for connections sharing the same output port, a cell or frame on a connection with a higher priority is much more likely to leave the switch before one on a connection with a lower priority, if both are in the switch at the same time. The number of priorities that each port of the switch supports may be obtained from the port configuration message.

The QoS Profile Model provides a simple mechanism that allows a connection to be assigned QoS semantics defined externally to GSMP, and it can be used to indicate pre-defined Differentiated Service per-hop behaviours. The definition of QoS profiles is outside the scope of the specification.

All GSMP switches must support the default QoS Configuration, and a switch may additionally support one or more alternative QoS Configurations whose QoS models are defined outside the GSMP specification. GSMP includes a negotiation mechanism that allows a controller to select from the QoS configurations that a switch supports. Traffic parameters are expressed in a common format, with a separate encoding for each of the service families, and the traffic controls are carried as flags, in one set for the input direction and one for the output direction.
sections.plainLanguage: Quality of service is the part of a connection that says how it should be treated. GSMP offers three ways to say it: name a service from a standard the switch already knows, give the connection a priority number, or point at a profile defined elsewhere. Every switch must offer the default set, and a controller can ask which alternatives the switch supports before choosing.

sections.title: The Adjacency Protocol
sections.content:
The adjacency protocol is used to synchronise state across the link, to agree on which version of the protocol to use, to discover the identity of the entity at the other end of a link, and to detect when it changes. GSMP is a hard state protocol, so it is important to detect loss of contact between switch and controller and to detect any change of identity of either. No GSMP messages other than those of the adjacency protocol may be sent across the link until the adjacency protocol has achieved synchronisation.

Adjacency messages have their own format. They carry a Version field used for version negotiation, a Message Type of 10, a Timer field, an M flag and a Code field that determines the function of the message, then the Sender Name and Receiver Name, the Sender Port and Receiver Port, a PType and PFlag, the Sender Instance and Receiver Instance, and the Partition ID.

Version negotiation is performed before synchronisation is achieved. In a SYN message the Version field always contains the highest version understood by the sender. A receiver that gets a SYN with a version higher than it understands ignores the message, and a receiver that gets a SYN with a lower version that it does understand replies with a SYNACK carrying the version from the received SYN. That defines the version of GSMP to be used while the adjacency protocol remains synchronised, and all other messages use the agreed version. The version number for the protocol defined by this specification is 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else can be said, the two ends introduce themselves and agree which version of the protocol to speak. Until that has happened, any other GSMP message is thrown away, and the two ends watch each other's name so that a link coming back with different equipment behind it is noticed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of the GSMP TCP/IP control channel is addressed in the document that specifies the packet encapsulations for GSMP. For all uses of GSMP over an IP network it is required that GSMP be run over TCP/IP using the security considerations discussed there.

The point is not hard to see. The controller can create, move and delete every connection in the switch, and the switch reports its whole state, so an unprotected control channel is a channel through which an outsider could take over the forwarding of the network. The rest of the protocol adds its own protection for that case: a message with the wrong port session number must be rejected, and no message other than an adjacency message may be sent until the two ends are synchronised.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is short here because the work is done elsewhere: the control channel itself has to be secured, and the rules for that are in the document that covers how GSMP is carried over TCP/IP. What this document adds is the check that a message carries the right port session number, so a message from a stale or forged session is refused.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: The GSMP protocol version agreed by the adjacency protocol.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: The kind of message, drawn from the classes the protocol defines.

fields.name: Result
fields.desc: Whether a response is expected, and in a response whether it succeeded.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: An error code in a failure response; unused in a request.

fields.name: Partition ID
fields.desc: Associates the command with a specific switch partition.

fields.name: Transaction Identifier
fields.desc: Associates a request message with its response message.

fields.name: I
fields.desc: When set, the submessage number field holds the total count of segments.

fields.name: SubMessage Number
fields.desc: The position of this segment within the whole message.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: The length of the message including its header and body.

items.label: NoSuccessAck
items.desc: The request does not expect a response if it succeeds.

items.label: AckAll
items.desc: A response is expected if the request succeeds.

items.label: Success
items.desc: A successful response, possibly the last of several messages.

items.label: Failure
items.desc: The request failed; the Code field says why.

items.label: More
items.desc: The message exceeds the link's maximum transmission unit and more will follow.

items.label: ReturnReceipt
items.desc: Used in event messages, where an acknowledgement is required.

items.title: Add Branch
items.text: Establishes a connection or adds a branch to one; message type 16.

items.title: Delete Branches
items.text: Removes branches; the one message that has its own response format; message type 17.

items.title: Delete Tree
items.text: Removes a whole multicast tree; message type 18.

items.title: Delete All Input
items.text: Removes every connection arriving on an input port; message type 20.

items.title: Move Output Branch
items.text: Moves an output branch to a different output port; message type 22.

items.title: Move Input Branch
items.text: Moves an input branch to a different input port; message type 23.

items.title: Synchronise state
items.text: No other GSMP message may be sent until the two ends are synchronised.

items.title: Agree the version
items.text: The SYN carries the highest version the sender understands, and the SYNACK carries the version they will use.

items.title: Discover the peer
items.text: The sender and receiver names and ports identify the entity at the other end of the link.

items.title: Detect a change
items.text: GSMP is a hard state protocol, so a change of identity or a loss of contact must be noticed.
